question: When cancer treatment cannot cure the disease, but aims to stop tumor growth and extend life, what is this main goal called?
explanation: You've got this! When complete cure isn't possible, 'control' is the goal—stopping the cancer from spreading further to help the patient live a longer, fuller life. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T8#GNS321_U1_T8_h1)

question: Why might a cancer care plan shift from trying to cure the disease to focusing purely on comfort and palliation?

options.A: Standard surgical options are suddenly much safer than outpatient chemotherapy.
options.B: The patient's insurance policy has expired and can no longer cover active medications.
options.C: The nursing staff prefers managing comfort care over administering toxic drugs.
options.D: The disease has progressed beyond the point where a cure or control is realistically achievable.

explanation: Spot on! When the disease advances past where treatment can stop it, the healthcare team shifts gears to palliation—focusing entirely on comfort, symptom relief, and quality of life. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T8#GNS321_U1_T8_h1)

question: What kind of surgery involves removing a healthy organ because a patient has a high genetic risk of getting cancer there later?
explanation: Great thinking! Prophylactic means preventative. Doctors perform this to remove healthy tissue before cancer ever gets a chance to start. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T8#GNS321_U1_T8_h2)

question: A patient has surgery to remove a bowel tumor just to relieve an active intestinal blockage. What type of surgery is this?
explanation: Well done! Even though it's surgery, it's classified as palliative because its main job is to ease distressing symptoms (like a blockage) rather than cure the cancer itself. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T8#GNS321_U1_T8_h2)

question: How does external radiation therapy mainly work to destroy cancer cells?

options.A: By chemically dissolving the outer cell wall
options.B: By starving the tumor of blood supply
options.C: By boosting the patient's native immune system
options.D: By damaging the internal DNA of the cells

explanation: You're doing great! Radiation targets the heart of the cell—its DNA—breaking it down so the cancer cells can no longer multiply. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T8#GNS321_U1_T8_h3)

question: Why do nurses constantly remind patients receiving radiation therapy not to wash off their skin treatment marks?

options.A: To prevent the patient from developing a severe skin allergy to the ink
options.B: To keep the hospital records accurate for billing and insurance purposes
options.C: To allow the radiation oncologists to track how fast the outer tumor is shrinking
options.D: To ensure precise daily alignment of the radiation beam to the exact tumor site

explanation: Spot on! Those little marks are like a bullseye. They make sure the radiation machine hits the exact tumor spot safely every single time. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T8#GNS321_U1_T8_h3)

question: What nursing term describes when a harsh chemotherapy drug accidentally leaks out of the vein into the surrounding tissue?
explanation: You've got this! Extravasation happens when a vesicant drug escapes into surrounding tissues, which can cause serious local tissue damage. Always protect your IV sites! [learn more](GNS321_U1_T8#GNS321_U1_T8_h4)

question: Why do patients on standard chemotherapy often experience hair loss and mouth sores?

options.A: The chemical makeup of the drugs directly dries out the outer layers of human skin.
options.B: The radiation energy absorbed by the bloodstream weakens oral and scalp tissues.
options.C: Patients naturally stop eating enough fresh fruits and vegetables due to nausea.
options.D: The medications attack all rapidly dividing cells, including healthy normal cells like hair follicles and mucosal linings.

explanation: Exactly! Chemotherapy targets fast-growing cells. Sadly, it can't tell the difference between cancer cells and our healthy fast-growing cells, like hair and gut linings. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T8#GNS321_U1_T8_h4)

question: What is the main way targeted cancer therapy drugs fight the disease?

options.A: They physically trap circulating tumor cells inside the liver.
options.B: They emit local ionizing radiation directly inside the blood vessels.
options.C: They replace the patient's damaged bone marrow with healthy donor cells.
options.D: They block specific molecules and growth pathways unique to cancer cells.

explanation: Brilliant! Unlike regular chemo, targeted therapy acts like a smart missile, zeroing in on specific chemical signals that tumors use to grow. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T8#GNS321_U1_T8_h5)

question: What is a major risk for patients taking immune checkpoint inhibitors (immunotherapy)?

options.A: The medication causes immediate permanent sterility in both male and female patients.
options.B: The boosted immune system may attack normal, healthy organs, causing widespread inflammation.
options.C: The drug destroys bone marrow production completely, requiring lifelong platelet transfusions.
options.D: The patient will instantly lose all hair follicles within forty-eight hours of the first dose.

explanation: You got it! Reviving the immune system is great for fighting cancer, but sometimes the revved-up immune cells accidentally attack healthy organs like the lungs or gut. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T8#GNS321_U1_T8_h5)

question: Which emergency shows up as facial swelling, upper body congestion, and swollen neck veins because a major blood vessel is blocked?
explanation: Awesome work! When a tumor presses on the superior vena cava, blood backs up from the upper body, causing that classic facial and neck swelling. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T8#GNS321_U1_T8_h6)

question: A cancer patient on chemo has a fever of 38.5°C and a very low neutrophil count. What is your immediate priority action?

options.A: Wait for routine morning blood cultures to return before calling the physician.
options.B: Administer prescribed broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics immediately.
options.C: Encourage the patient to drink large volumes of cold citrus juices.
options.D: Apply an ice blanket to bring down the patient's core body temperature.

explanation: Safety first! Febrile neutropenia is a life-threatening emergency. Quick IV antibiotics are vital to stop rapid-fire sepsis in its tracks. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T8#GNS321_U1_T8_h6)

question: When assessing a patient's pain, what is always considered the most reliable indicator?

options.A: The physical size and location of the tumor
options.B: The observable heart rate and blood pressure

explanation: Spot on, future nurse! Pain is subjective. If the patient says it hurts, it hurts—their word is always our gold standard for assessment. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T8#GNS321_U1_T8_h7)

question: Why do nurses give anti-nausea (antiemetic) medications *before* chemotherapy starts, instead of waiting for nausea to begin?

options.A: Chemotherapy drugs lose their chemical potency if antiemetics are not circulating beforehand.
options.B: Patients will refuse their chemotherapy infusions entirely if they feel even a slight hint of nausea.
options.C: Proactive antiemetic dosing ensures the patient remains fast asleep throughout the entire procedure.
options.D: It is much easier to prevent nausea from developing than to stop it once it has already started.

explanation: You're totally right! Prevention is key here. Stopping nausea signals before they trigger makes treatment way more tolerable for the patient. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T8#GNS321_U1_T8_h7)

question: At what point in their journey can a cancer patient start receiving palliative care?

options.A: When the patient's life expectancy drops below two weeks
options.B: Once the patient is admitted to a dedicated hospice facility
options.C: At the time of diagnosis, alongside active curative treatments
options.D: Only after all forms of chemotherapy and radiation have failed

explanation: Brilliant! Palliative care isn't just for end-of-life; it can—and should—start right from diagnosis to help manage symptoms while active treatment happens. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T8#GNS321_U1_T8_h8)

question: How does general palliative care differ from standard hospice care?

options.A: Palliative care is only provided in outpatient clinics, while hospice care is strictly for hospital inpatients.
options.B: Palliative care can be given alongside curative treatments, whereas hospice care begins when curative treatment has stopped.
options.C: Palliative care is managed entirely by physicians, whereas hospice care is run strictly by volunteers.
options.D: Palliative care focuses exclusively on spiritual counseling, while hospice care manages physical pain.

explanation: You nailed it! Think of hospice as a specific type of palliative care reserved for the final phase of life, while general palliative care can start on day one. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T8#GNS321_U1_T8_h8)
